answer_text: The house I grew up in was a single-story brick house in a small village, and looking back, it shaped a lot of my childhood. Three generations lived under one roof, so it was never quiet, but I loved that. The most important part of the house wasn't even inside—it was the front yard. We had a mango tree there, and in summer my cousins and I would climb it, which drove my grandmother crazy. The house itself was basic. The kitchen was separate from the main building, and we used to cook with firewood until I was about ten. Compared to that, my apartment now is a completely different world. It's on the eighth floor, it has modern appliances, and I can get almost anything I need within five minutes. Practically speaking, it's much easier to live in. What I've lost, though, is that sense of community. Back then, neighbors would just walk into our yard to chat, whereas now I barely know the people on my floor. So if you asked me which one is better, I'd say my apartment fits the life I have now, but my old house gave me memories I wouldn't trade for anything.

Nobody littered, people queued patiently, and the streets felt designed for pedestrians rather than motorbikes. The moment I'll never forget, though, was getting lost on the last night. My phone had died, and a woman I asked for directions ended up walking me ten minutes to the station. That small act completely changed how I felt about traveling alone. Since then, I've been to a few other countries, but that first trip gave me the confidence to go.

answer_text: The biggest holiday in my country is definitely Tet, or the Lunar New Year. It usually falls in late January or February, and it's basically the Vietnamese version of Christmas and New Year combined. The preparation starts weeks before. People clean their houses from top to bottom, because they believe it sweeps away bad luck from the old year. Then they decorate with peach blossoms in the north or yellow apricot flowers in the south. One of the most important traditions is making banh chung, which is a square sticky rice cake with pork and green beans inside. In my family, we still wrap them together at my parents' house. On the first days of the new year, we visit relatives, give lucky money to the kids, and wish everyone health and success. What I love most about Tet is that no matter how far away people work, they try to come home. The roads are crazy, but the feeling of being together is worth it.

answer_text: In Vietnam there's no question that the most important holiday is Tet, the Lunar New Year. It moves every year because it follows the lunar calendar, but it's usually somewhere between late January and mid-February. For foreigners, I usually describe it as Christmas, New Year's, and Thanksgiving rolled into one, because it's about family, food, and a fresh start all at once. The run-up is honestly the busiest time of the year. Offices rush to finish everything, and at home people do a deep clean, partly for practical reasons and partly because there's a belief that you should sweep out the bad luck of the old year before the new one begins. Markets fill up with peach blossoms in the north and yellow apricot blossoms in the south, and in a lot of families, including mine, we still wrap banh chung together, which takes almost a whole day. The first three days of the year have their own rhythm. The first day is usually for the father's side of the family, the second for the mother's side, and the third for teachers or friends. Kids receive lucky money in red envelopes, and everyone tries to say only positive things. Even though Tet has become more commercial lately, I think its core—people traveling hundreds of kilometers just to sit down together for a meal—hasn't changed at all.

Since becoming a dad, I've watched more animated films than I can count, and some of them handle emotions better than most adult movies. So my answer is action for myself, animation with my family, and dramas only when I'm in the right mood, which isn't very often.

answer_text: The one I still think about is the morning of my job interview four years ago—for the position I have now, which makes it a bit funny in hindsight. I'd done everything right, or so I thought. I'd checked the route the day before, ironed my shirt, and planned to leave an hour and a half early. What I took from it is that you can't control everything, but you can control how you communicate when things go wrong.

Most people still mainly called and texted, and if you wanted to go online, the connection was often slow and expensive, so people waited until they had Wi-Fi. Social media was popular, but it was mostly about posting photos and chatting with friends. Today, I'd say there are three big changes. First, phones have replaced a lot of other things. People use them as wallets, cameras, maps, and even as their main computer. Second, the way we pay has changed completely. In Vietnam now, you can pay for almost anything with a QR code, even at a street food stall. And third, phones have become work tools. My coworkers and I share reports and updates through group chats every day, which was unusual ten years ago. Overall, phones make life much more convenient, but I think people are also more dependent on them than ever.

answer_text: I think the biggest concern people have these days is online scams. In Vietnam, there are a lot of fake calls and messages pretending to be from banks or delivery companies. For example, last year one of my neighbors got a message saying her package was stuck and she had to pay a small fee. She clicked the link, and then someone took money from her bank account. Stories like that make people really nervous. The second concern is privacy. Many apps ask for access to your contacts, photos, and location, and people don't really know where that information goes. Because of these worries, people have changed how they use the internet. Older people especially are more careful about answering unknown calls, and a lot of people now use two-step verification for their bank apps. Personally, I think the most important thing is education. If people know the common tricks, they're much less likely to fall for them.

answer_text: I'd say there are two main worries, and they're connected. The first, and the one people talk about most, is fraud. As more of daily life has moved online—banking, shopping, even paying for parking—scammers have followed. In Vietnam, a very common trick is a message that looks like it's from a bank or a delivery company, asking you to click a link to fix a problem. A neighbor of mine lost a fair amount of money that way last year, and what struck me was how convincing the message looked. The second worry is privacy in a broader sense. A lot of apps collect far more data than they need, and when there's a leak, people suddenly realize their phone number or address is circulating somewhere. The two are linked, because leaked data is often what makes scams so believable. These concerns have definitely changed behavior. People are more suspicious of unknown calls, banks have added extra verification steps, and some of my older relatives now refuse to do anything financial online, which, honestly, isn't a solution either. In my view, the answer has to come from both sides. Companies need to collect less and protect more, and individuals, especially older people, need simple, practical training rather than just warnings.

answer_text: I think the difference is quite big. For my parents' generation, being a little chubby was actually a sign of good health. They grew up at a time when food wasn't always easy to get, so if someone looked thin, people would worry about them. My mom still tells me I've lost weight every time she sees me, even when I haven't. They also didn't think about exercise much, because most of them did physical work every day anyway. My generation sees it differently. A lot of people my age go to the gym, track their steps, and pay attention to things like sugar and calories. We also talk much more openly about mental health and stress, which my parents almost never mentioned. That said, there are some similarities. Both generations believe in home-cooked meals, and my parents' habit of going to bed early is something I'm actually trying to copy. So I'd say each generation has something to learn from the other.

answer_text: I'd say the two generations started from very different places, which explains a lot. My parents grew up in a period when food was limited, so for them, being well-fed was the clearest sign of health. Being a bit heavy meant you were doing fine, and being thin meant something was wrong. You can still hear it today—my mom comments on my weight every single visit, usually telling me I look too skinny. Exercise wasn't really a concept for them either, because their daily lives were already physically demanding. My generation, on the other hand, grew up with more food than we need and jobs where we sit all day, so health has become something we actively manage. People my age go to the gym, count steps, read nutrition labels, and, importantly, talk about mental health, which was almost taboo for my parents. But I don't think my generation has it all figured out. Social media has pushed a very narrow idea of what a healthy body looks like, and some young people take dieting to unhealthy extremes. Meanwhile, my parents' habits—cooking at home, sleeping early, walking everywhere—were actually very healthy, even if they didn't call it that. So if anything, I think the ideal would be a mix of both.
